claims.source: In the true change condition, but in neither of the sham conditions, mice slowed their approach (Figure 2c, p<0.005 change vs. only before, and p<0.01 change vs. only after, rank sum), presumably to precisely re-locate the target before crossing, showing that mice perceive and react to the sensory deviant.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the differential behavioral response to true change vs. sham change conditions.

claims.claim: Weak L6 drive removed the deceleration associated with platform position deviants.
claims.source: We next tested whether the weaker L6 optogenetic drive (<1 mW) would impair this change detection behavior, and found that it removed the extra sampling time that platform motion would otherwise generate (p<0.001 laser vs. control, N = 317 trials, Figure 2d,e, Video 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 2d,e showing loss of deceleration with statistical significance p<0.001.

claims.claim: Weak L6 drive did not affect behavior when the target platform was static.
claims.source: Weak L6 drive did not affect behavior when the target platform was static (p=0.9, N = 751 trials, Figure 2f,g, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 2f,g showing no significant difference (p=0.9).

claims.claim: Weak L6 drive slightly increased the overall likelihood of crossing.
claims.source: The weaker drive also slightly increased the overall likelihood of crossing (Figure 1d, same analysis as Figure 1c).
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1d.

claims.claim: Gap Crossing is sensitive to changes in sensory function.
claims.source: Gap Crossing is sensitive to changes in sensory function (Celikel and Sakmann, 2007; Chaudhary and Rema, 2018), the maintenance of regular Gap Crossing behavior in the static platform condition indicates that weak L6 CT drive did not impact basic sensory function, but did impact change detection.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Celikel and Sakmann, 2007 and Chaudhary and Rema, 2018.

claims.claim: Weak L6 CT drive did not impact basic sensory function but did impact change detection.
claims.source: Gap Crossing is sensitive to changes in sensory function (Celikel and Sakmann, 2007; Chaudhary and Rema, 2018), the maintenance of regular Gap Crossing behavior in the static platform condition indicates that weak L6 CT drive did not impact basic sensory function, but did impact change detection.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the selective effect on deviant trials but not baseline trials.

claims.claim: Platform position deviants in Gap Crossing likely result from changes in multiple sensory parameters including amplitude of vibrissal contact deflections.
claims.source: Detecting a sudden change in platform position in the Gap Crossing with Deviation experiment likely results from a combination of multiple sensory parameters that change because of the changed position of the vibrissa contacts. Previous high-speed videography studies under the same experimental conditions showed that these parameters include a change in amplitude of vibrissal contact deflections (Voigts et al., 2015), as well as other parameters such as relative timing (Voigts et al., 2015), and likely deflection angles (Knutsen et al., 2008; Ritt et al., 2008), assymetry (Dominiak et al., 2019), time course of the torque (Pammer et al., 2013), and vibrations (Ritt et al., 2008; Lottem and Azouz, 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies characterizing vibrissal mechanics.

claims.claim: Deviants increased the detection rate for threshold level stimuli in head-fixed detection task.
claims.source: A subset of these trains contained direction deviants (Figure 3a), though mice were not trained to report the presence of a deviant. Deviants increased the detection rate for threshold level stimuli (Figure 3a,b).
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3a,b.

claims.claim: Weak L6 drive removed the behavioral benefit of direction deviants in head-fixed detection.
claims.source: Weak L6 drive removed this effect but had no impact on detection of stimuli containing no deviant.
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 3b showing loss of deviant benefit under laser condition.

claims.claim: Weak L6 drive had no impact on detection of stimuli containing no deviant.
claims.source: Weak L6 drive removed this effect but had no impact on detection of stimuli containing no deviant.
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 3b showing no change in baseline detection.

claims.claim: Weak L6 drive disrupted encoding of deflection direction in L6.
claims.source: We also observed that weak L6 drive disrupted encoding of deflection direction in L6 and of deviant stimuli in L2/3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by imaging and electrophysiology data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Weak L6 drive disrupted encoding of deviant stimuli in L2/3.
claims.source: We also observed that weak L6 drive disrupted encoding of deflection direction in L6 and of deviant stimuli in L2/3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Strong L6 CT optogenetic activation recruits trans-laminar inhibition and reduces neocortical sensory gain in V1.
claims.source: We tested mice on the Gap Crossing task under two conditions, strong L6 CT optogenetic activation (>2 mW power) that recruits trans-laminar inhibition and reduces neocortical sensory gain in V1 (Olsen et al., 2012), or weak L6 drive (<1 mW) (Figure 1a).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Olsen et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Strong optogenetic drive of L6 reduces sensory gain in SI.
claims.source: Prior studies have shown that strong L6 drive reduces sensory gain (Olsen et al., 2012; Denman and Contreras, 2015) in V1, and we observed analogous suppression in SI when we drove L6 with the strong optogenetic stimulus (Figure 4a, acute laminar probe recording).
claims.evidence: Supported by data in Figure 4a and citations to Olsen et al., 2012 and Denman and Contreras, 2015.

claims.claim: L6 neurons were sparsely sensory responsive, with only ~13% being phasically sensory driven.
claims.source: Consistent with prior studies (Thomson, 2010; Lee et al., 2008; Swadlow and Hicks, 1996), L6 neurons were sparsely sensory responsive, as only 18 (RS and FS) of 139 (~13%) were phasically sensory driven.
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings and citations to Thomson, 2010; Lee et al., 2008; Swadlow and Hicks, 1996.

claims.claim: Driven L6 neurons showed only small vibrissa-driven increases in their activity.
claims.source: Further, driven L6 neurons were also sparse in their response rates, showing only small vibrissa-driven increases in their activity (Figure 4b).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4b.

claims.claim: Weak L6 drive did not impact sensory-evoked firing rates in RS from any layer.
claims.source: In contrast to stronger drive, this stimulus did not impact sensory-evoked firing rates in RS from any layer (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 4b and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Weak L6 drive caused a modest decrease in sensory responses in L4 FS.
claims.source: The only significant impact on sensory responses was a modest decrease in sensory responses in L4 FS (31.7 vs. 24.6 Hz median peak rates, p=0.001, Figure 4b).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 4b with statistical significance p=0.001.

claims.claim: A small increase in firing rates in non-sensory-responsive L6 FS was observed with weak L6 drive.
claims.source: A small increase in firing rates in non-sensory-responsive L6 FS was also observed (Figure 4b, p=0.02 sign-rank, laser - control firing rates, N = 37).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 4b with statistical significance p=0.02.

claims.claim: Increased activity in L6 FS presumably offset the direct effects of optogenetic drive in L6 RS, keeping L6 RS firing rates at baseline level.
claims.source: Increased activity in these L6 FS presumably offset the direct effects of optogenetic drive in L6 RS, keeping L6 RS firing rates at a baseline level (p=0.18, N = 89, signed rank).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the balance between excitatory drive and inhibitory compensation, supported by non-significant change in L6 RS rates (p=0.18).

claims.claim: In L2/3 and L5 RS, transient suppression was evident after optogenetic stimulus onset, but rates returned to baseline prior to sensory stimulation.
claims.source: In L2/3 and L5 RS, transient suppression was evident after optogenetic stimulus onset, but rates returned to baseline prior to sensory stimulation.
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data showing temporal dynamics of firing rates.

claims.claim: Weak optogenetic drive did not change the mean population response of L6 to sensory input.
claims.source: Optogenetic drive did not significantly change the mean population response of L6 to sensory input, ranksum test, CI via bootstrap of median.
claims.evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data shown in Figure 5f with statistical test.

claims.claim: Individual L6 cells showed significant facilitation or suppression of vibrissa-evoked responses during optogenetic drive.
claims.source: However, individual L6 cells showed significant facilitation or suppression of vibrissa-evoked responses during optogenetic drive.
claims.evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data shown in Figure 5g.

claims.claim: Optogenetic L6 activation shifted the identity of the activated ensemble.
claims.source: Optogenetic L6 activation did not change the overall output from L6, but shifted the identity of the activated ensemble (p<0.001 IQR vs. shuffled control), regardless of whether cells were classified as vibrissa-driven in the control (red) or in the laser (blue) condition.
claims.evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data in Figure 5h with statistical significance p<0.001.

claims.claim: Of L6 cells that were sensory responsive in the laser condition, 25.0% were significantly facilitated and 23.9% suppressed.
claims.source: Of cells that were sensory responsive in the laser condition, 25.0% were significantly facilitated, 23.9% suppressed, and of cells sensory responsive in the control condition, 10.9% were facilitated, 32.9% suppressed.
claims.evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data analysis shown in Figure 5h.

claims.claim: Of L6 cells that were sensory responsive in the control condition, 10.9% were facilitated and 32.9% suppressed.
claims.source: Of cells that were sensory responsive in the laser condition, 25.0% were significantly facilitated, 23.9% suppressed, and of cells sensory responsive in the control condition, 10.9% were facilitated, 32.9% suppressed.
claims.evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data analysis shown in Figure 5h.

claims.claim: Variations in stimulus amplitude without deviants were not encoded in the mean firing rates of L4 RS cells.
claims.source: Variations in stimulus amplitude (without deviants) were not encoded in the mean firing rates of layer 4 (L4) or L2/3 RS cells (L4 N = 37 RS; spike count difference between larger and smaller stimuli, signed rank p=0.221, 95% confidence interval (CI): [−0.22, 0, 0.002], L2/3 N = 94, p=0.201, CI:[−0.009,–0.003,0], Figure 6a–c).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 6a-c with statistical tests showing non-significance.

claims.claim: Variations in stimulus amplitude without deviants were not encoded in the mean firing rates of L2/3 RS cells.
claims.source: Variations in stimulus amplitude (without deviants) were not encoded in the mean firing rates of layer 4 (L4) or L2/3 RS cells (L4 N = 37 RS; spike count difference between larger and smaller stimuli, signed rank p=0.221, 95% confidence interval (CI): [−0.22, 0, 0.002], L2/3 N = 94, p=0.201, CI:[−0.009,–0.003,0], Figure 6a–c).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 6a-c with statistical tests showing non-significance.

claims.claim: Small variations in overall stimulus strength were not reliably encoded in SI.
claims.source: Small variations in overall stimulus strength were therefore not reliably encoded in SI.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the lack of significant encoding in L4 and L2/3 RS cells.

claims.claim: Neither L2/3 nor L4 neurons systematically increased their overall firing rates for deviants when amplitude increases and decreases were grouped together.
claims.source: While individual neurons displayed such sensitivity to deviation (Figure 6d), neither L2/3 nor L4 neurons systematically increased their overall firing rates for deviants when amplitude increases and decreases were grouped together (Figure 6e), showing that our stimulus design avoided pre-cortical stimulus-specific adaptation (Movshon and Lennie, 1979).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 6e showing no systematic rate increase.

claims.claim: The stimulus design avoided pre-cortical stimulus-specific adaptation.
claims.source: While individual neurons displayed such sensitivity to deviation (Figure 6d), neither L2/3 nor L4 neurons systematically increased their overall firing rates for deviants when amplitude increases and decreases were grouped together (Figure 6e), showing that our stimulus design avoided pre-cortical stimulus-specific adaptation (Movshon and Lennie, 1979).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the lack of overall rate increase for deviants, with reference to Movshon and Lennie, 1979.

claims.claim: L4 neurons consistently showed positive change coefficients, firing more spikes for deviant increases and fewer for decreases.
claims.source: L4 neurons consistently showed positive change coefficients, firing more spikes for deviant increases and fewer for decreases. This encoding is evident at the population level as a rightward shift in the distribution of change coefficients (Figure 7b, p=0.005, CI:[0.012, 0.016, 0.035]; See Figure 9—figure supplement 1 for generalized linear model 'GLM' analysis).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 7b with statistical significance p=0.005.

claims.claim: Spike count differences for deviations in L4 were larger than for equivalent variations in baseline amplitude with no deviant.
claims.source: These spike count differences for deviations were larger than for equivalent variations in baseline amplitude with no deviant (p=0.016, signed rank).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical comparison with p=0.016.

claims.claim: No significant deviant encoding was observed in L5.
claims.source: We observed no significant deviant encoding in L5 (N = 92: p>0.05).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data showing non-significant results (p>0.05).

claims.claim: L4 findings can be interpreted as enhanced specificity of encoding following an adapting stimulus.
claims.source: These findings in L4 can be interpreted as enhanced specificity of encoding following an adapting stimulus, as observed across several stimulus types (Ollerenshaw et al., 2014; Moore et al., 1999; Andermann et al., 2004), in this case amplitude encoding.
claims.evidence: Interpretation supported by citations to Ollerenshaw et al., 2014; Moore et al., 1999; Andermann et al., 2004.

claims.claim: The increased sensitivity of amplitude encoding in L4 after adaptation is consistent with enhanced discriminability of stimulus features generally observed with adaptation.
claims.source: This increased sensitivity of amplitude encoding in L4 after adaptation to a baseline is consistent with the enhanced discriminability of stimulus features generally observed with adaptation (Ollerenshaw et al., 2014; Békésy, 1967; Tannan et al., 2006; Abbott et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Ollerenshaw et al., 2014; Békésy, 1967; Tannan et al., 2006; Abbott et al., 1997.

claims.claim: A subset of L2/3 neurons showed positive change encoding, but negative change coefficients were also observed.
claims.source: As in L4, a subset of L2/3 neurons showed positive change encoding, but negative change coefficients were also observed, i.e. neurons with greater firing in response to stimulus decreases (Figure 7a, examples ii and iii).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7a.

claims.claim: The L2/3 change coefficient distribution was significantly broader than the surrogate distribution.
claims.source: The observed distribution was significantly broader than the surrogate (interquartile range/IQR; Figure 7c; p=0.006, Shannon entropy: p=0.029, via bootstrapping, see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data in Figure 7c with p=0.006 for IQR and p=0.029 for entropy.

claims.claim: L2/3 RS continued to represent change from stimulus history with a broadened distribution when deviant amplitude was fixed.
claims.source: With fixed deviant amplitude, L2/3 RS continued to represent change from stimulus history with a broadened distribution (Figure 7d; IQR p=0.004, entropy p=0.014, N = 87), showing that L2/3 RS cells encode history dependent heterogeneous change signals.
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 7d with statistical significance.

claims.claim: L2/3 RS cells encode history dependent heterogeneous change signals.
claims.source: With fixed deviant amplitude, L2/3 RS continued to represent change from stimulus history with a broadened distribution (Figure 7d; IQR p=0.004, entropy p=0.014, N = 87), showing that L2/3 RS cells encode history dependent heterogeneous change signals.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the persistence of broadened distribution when deviant amplitude is fixed but preceded by different baseline amplitudes.

claims.claim: L4 neurons encode deviant amplitude, reflected in a positive correlation between their rates and the direction of amplitude change.
claims.source: In sum, L4 neurons encode deviant amplitude, reflected in a positive correlation between their rates and the direction of amplitude change.
claims.evidence: Summary of findings from electrophysiological data in Figure 7.

claims.claim: L2/3 neurons showed a variety of responses to deviants, with different receptive fields for specific patterns of baseline and deviant.
claims.source: In contrast, L2/3 neurons showed a variety of responses to deviants, with different receptive fields for specific patterns of baseline and deviant (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 7 showing heterogeneous responses.

claims.claim: Only ~13% of L6 neurons were stimulus-driven in 2-photon imaging experiments.
claims.source: Consistent with electrophysiological data, L6 activity was sparse, as only ~13% of L6 neurons were stimulus-driven (469/3408 cells, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: L6 CT cells encoded baseline amplitude, with significantly higher integrated calcium signals for larger stimuli.
claims.source: When stimuli without deviants were presented, L6 CT cells encoded baseline amplitude, with significantly higher integrated calcium signals for larger stimuli (p<0.001 signed rank, N = 346, Figure 8).
claims.evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data in Figure 8 with statistical significance p<0.001.

claims.claim: L6 CT encoded amplitude differences when deviants were presented after 400 ms.
claims.source: As with baseline amplitude variations, L6 CT also encoded these amplitude differences (p<0.001, Figure 8).
claims.evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data in Figure 8 with statistical significance p<0.001.

claims.claim: L6 CT encoded stimulus amplitude as a variation in relative firing rate, which could serve as a baseline for a change-detection computation.
claims.source: Nevertheless, these data show that L6 CT encoded stimulus amplitude as a variation in relative firing rate, which could serve as a baseline for a change-detection computation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the amplitude encoding observed in L6 CT cells.

claims.claim: Weak optogenetic drive removed the encoding of stimulus amplitude in L6 CT.
claims.source: We found that weak optogenetic drive removed the encoding of stimulus amplitude (Figure 9d,e, p<0.05, ranksum, evoked ΔF/F change between stimuli, control vs. laser).
claims.evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data in Figure 9d,e with statistical significance p<0.05.

claims.claim: Both the identity of the sensory-driven ensemble and amplitude encoding by L6 CT was disrupted by weak optogenetic drive.
claims.source: In sum, both the identity of the sensory-driven ensemble and amplitude encoding by L6 CT was disrupted by weak optogenetic drive, despite no change in the net activity in these neurons.
claims.evidence: Summary of findings from 2-photon imaging data in Figures 5, 8, and 9.

claims.claim: Weak L6 CT drive caused a loss in the heterogeneity of L2/3 encoding of deviants.
claims.source: Across the L2/3 population, weak L6 CT drive caused a loss in the heterogeneity of L2/3 encoding of deviants, reflected as a sharpening of the distribution and a bias to positive change coefficients, paralleling L4 encoding.
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 9b showing distribution changes.

claims.claim: Change representation in L2/3 was disrupted by weak optogenetic drive of L6.
claims.source: We found that change representation in L2/3 was disrupted (Figure 9b, p=0.010 entropy reduction, p=0.020 IQR reduction, p=0.008 paired left tailed IQR, N = 94).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 9b with multiple statistical measures.

claims.claim: During optogenetic drive, L2/3 neurons came to represent current stimulus amplitudes with positive change coefficients and reduced their history-dependence.
claims.source: During optogenetic drive, L2/3 neurons came to represent current stimulus amplitudes with positive change coefficients (CI: [0.002, 0.009, 0.016], p=0.003 signed rank) and reduced their history-dependence (Figure 9, p=0.014 entropy reduction, p=0.004 IQR reduction, p=0.043 paired left tailed IQR).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 9 with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Shuffling the active L6 ensemble removed the change-specific receptive fields in L2/3, causing them to instead encode current stimuli, making them more similar to L4 cells.
claims.source: Shuffling the active L6 ensemble therefore removed the change-specific receptive fields in L2/3, causing them to instead encode current stimuli, making them more similar to L4 cells.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the shift in L2/3 encoding properties under weak L6 drive.

claims.claim: Optogenetic drive of L6 impacts sensory responses in visual neocortex through an intracortical pathway, not by modulation of thalamic relay neurons.
claims.source: Recent studies have concluded that optogenetic drive of L6 impacts sensory responses in visual neocortex through an intracortical pathway, and not by modulation of thalamic relay neurons (Olsen et al., 2012; Bortone et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Olsen et al., 2012 and Bortone et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Of 240 well-isolated thalamic single units, 25 cells were phasically responsive at short latencies to vibrissal stimulation.
claims.source: Of 240 well-isolated thalamic single units (N = 3 mice), 25 cells were phasically responsive at short latencies to vibrissal stimulation.
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings from VPM.

claims.claim: VPM neurons showed weak rate increases with L6 optogenetic drive, in contrast to the suppression observed in prior studies using stronger L6 CT drive.
claims.source: These neurons showed weak rate increases with L6 optogenetic drive, in contrast to the suppression observed in prior studies using stronger L6 CT drive (Denman and Contreras, 2015; Bortone et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data from VPM recordings and citations to Denman and Contreras, 2015 and Bortone et al., 2014.

claims.claim: No significant encoding of deviants was observed in VPM, nor was modulation of encoding of deviants by L6 drive observed.
claims.source: However, no significant encoding of deviants was observed, nor was modulation of encoding of deviants by L6 drive observed (Figure 9—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 9—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Layers that receive direct lemniscal thalamic input (L4, L5, and L6) did not show explicit deviance encoding other than encoding of current stimulus amplitude.
claims.source: Further, as described above, layers that receive direct lemniscal thalamic input (L4, L5, and L6) did not show explicit deviance encoding other than encoding of current stimulus amplitude.
claims.evidence: Summary of findings from electrophysiological data across layers.

claims.claim: Evidence supports a local neocortical mechanism for the emergence of L2/3 deviant responses and their modulation under L6 optogenetic drive.
claims.source: These two forms of evidence, and prior studies finding a direct intracortical pathway as the primary route of influence by L6 CT (Bortone et al., 2014), supports a local neocortical mechanism for the emergence of L2/3 deviant responses and in their modulation under L6 optogenetic drive.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the combination of lack of thalamic deviance encoding and prior studies, with citation to Bortone et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Weak optogenetic drive of L6 CT substantially altered sensory encoding by L6 CT despite not altering overall firing rates.
claims.source: However, this weak optogenetic stimulus regime did substantially alter sensory encoding by L6 CT. These neurons lost their amplitude encoding, and many individual neurons showed changes in their sensory responsiveness, shifting the specific ensemble of L6 CT activated (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data in Figure 5 showing ensemble changes and loss of encoding.

claims.claim: L2/3 neurons lost their emergent heterogeneous encoding of deviants under weak L6 drive, showing instead the positive change encoding observed in L4 under normal conditions.
claims.source: Further, L2/3 neurons lost their emergent heterogeneous encoding of deviants, showing instead the positive change encoding observed in L4 under normal conditions (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 9.

claims.claim: Weak L6 drive selectively suppressed indicators of deviant processing in head-fixed and free behaviors.
claims.source: Weak L6 drive also selectively suppressed indicators of deviant processing in head-fixed (Figure 3) and free (Figures 1 and 2) behaviors.
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figures 1, 2, and 3.

claims.claim: Layer-specific encoding of deviants was observed.
claims.source: We observed layer-specific encoding of deviants and robust behavioral sensitivity to small stimulus deviations.
claims.evidence: Summary of findings from electrophysiological and behavioral data.

claims.claim: Robust behavioral sensitivity to small stimulus deviations was observed.
claims.source: We observed layer-specific encoding of deviants and robust behavioral sensitivity to small stimulus deviations.
claims.evidence: Summary of findings from behavioral data in Figures 2 and 3.

claims.claim: Small stimulus amplitude deviants were correlated positively with firing rates in L4 and L6.
claims.source: Small stimulus amplitude deviants were correlated positively with firing rates in L4 and L6, with deviant amplitude increases driving higher firing rates.
claims.evidence: Summary of findings from electrophysiological and imaging data in Figures 7 and 8.

claims.claim: Heterogeneous encoding emerged in L2/3 neurons, where cells could encode amplitude increases by decreases in rate.
claims.source: In contrast, heterogeneous encoding, where cells could, for example, encode amplitude increases by decreases in rate, and encoding of stimulus history, emerged in L2/3 neurons.
claims.evidence: Summary of findings from electrophysiological data in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Encoding of stimulus history emerged in L2/3 neurons.
claims.source: In contrast, heterogeneous encoding, where cells could, for example, encode amplitude increases by decreases in rate, and encoding of stimulus history, emerged in L2/3 neurons.
claims.evidence: Summary of findings from electrophysiological data in Figure 7d.

claims.claim: Weak optogenetic drive changed the sensory-responsive L6 ensemble by facilitating and suppressing different subsets of cells without changing overall firing rates.
claims.source: Weak optogenetic drive changed the sensory-responsive L6 ensemble, by facilitating and suppressing different subsets of cells without changing the overall firing rates and reduced their information content about the stimulus.
claims.evidence: Summary of findings from 2-photon imaging data in Figures 5 and 8.

claims.claim: Weak optogenetic drive reduced the information content of L6 about the stimulus.
claims.source: Weak optogenetic drive changed the sensory-responsive L6 ensemble, by facilitating and suppressing different subsets of cells without changing the overall firing rates and reduced their information content about the stimulus.
claims.evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data in Figure 8—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claims.claim: Detection of small stimulus deviations in the Gap Crossing with Deviants task was lost with weak L6 optogenetic drive without altering basic task performance.
claims.source: Detection of small stimulus deviations in the Gap Crossing with Deviants task, and the benefit of deviants for basic detection, were also lost with weak L6 optogenetic drive without altering basic task performance (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: Summary of behavioral findings shown in Figure 10.

claims.claim: The benefit of deviants for basic detection was lost with weak L6 optogenetic drive without altering basic task performance.
claims.source: Detection of small stimulus deviations in the Gap Crossing with Deviants task, and the benefit of deviants for basic detection, were also lost with weak L6 optogenetic drive without altering basic task performance (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: Summary of behavioral findings shown in Figure 10.

claims.claim: Stimulus encoding by sparse ensembles in L6 contributes to the neocortical circuit that processes sensory deviation but is not required for basic sensory function.
claims.source: These results indicate that stimulus encoding by sparse ensembles in L6 contributes to the neocortical circuit that processes sensory deviation but is not required for basic sensory function.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the selective effects on deviant processing but not baseline performance.

claims.claim: The weak L6 manipulation isolated a network mechanism or computation that is selectively involved in stimulus change processing, but not in processing of repeating, or predictable stimuli.
claims.source: The specific impact of the weak L6 manipulation on deviant encoding but not sensory gain (Figures 4 and 9), and on deviant-driven sensory behaviors but not basic performance (Figures 2 and 3), indicates that this intervention isolated a network mechanism or computation that is selectively involved in stimulus change processing, but not in processing of repeating, or predictable stimuli.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the pattern of selective effects across multiple measures.

claims.claim: The failure of weak L6 drive to impact baseline behavior contrasts with findings showing that subtle optogenetic manipulation in SI can affect baseline sensory detection behavior.
claims.source: The failure of weak L6 drive to impact baseline behavior is in contrast with several findings showing that relatively subtle optogenetic manipulation in SI, for example induced via similarly weak drive of PV+ interneurons (Sachidhanandam et al., 2013; Siegle et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2012) or L4 stellate neurons (O'Connor et al., 2013; Sofroniew et al., 2015), or direct stimulation of single neurons in other layers (Houweling and Brecht, 2008), can affect baseline sensory detection behavior.
claims.evidence: Comparison to prior literature supported by citations to Sachidhanandam et al., 2013; Siegle et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2012; O'Connor et al., 2013; Sofroniew et al., 2015; Houweling and Brecht, 2008.

claims.claim: The stimulus design minimized stimulus-specific adaptation.
claims.source: Here, we specifically sought to minimize such stimulus-specific adaptation.
claims.evidence: Stated experimental design goal, supported by lack of overall rate increase for deviants (Figure 6e).

claims.claim: The lack of stimulus-specific adaptation is evident in the lack of overall increase in firing rates for deviants.
claims.source: This lack of stimulus-specific adaptation is evident in the lack of overall increase in firing rates for deviants (Figure 6e).
claims.evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 6e.

claims.claim: The L6 CT cells imaged and controlled may affect cortical activity via recruitment of local and trans-laminar FS mediated inhibition.
claims.source: The L6 CT cells imaged and controlled in the present experiments may affect cortical activity via the recruitment of local (Zhang and Deschênes, 1997) and trans-laminar (Bortone et al., 2014) FS mediated inhibition, and through corticothalamic effects (Thomson, 2010; Denman and Contreras, 2015).
claims.evidence: Speculative mechanism supported by citations to Zhang and Deschênes, 1997; Bortone et al., 2014; Thomson, 2010; Denman and Contreras, 2015.

claims.claim: The L6 CT cells may affect cortical activity through corticothalamic effects.
claims.source: The L6 CT cells imaged and controlled in the present experiments may affect cortical activity via the recruitment of local (Zhang and Deschênes, 1997) and trans-laminar (Bortone et al., 2014) FS mediated inhibition, and through corticothalamic effects (Thomson, 2010; Denman and Contreras, 2015).
claims.evidence: Speculative mechanism supported by citations to Thomson, 2010 and Denman and Contreras, 2015.

claims.claim: The mechanisms by which specific ensembles of L6 cells influence state or stimulus encoding in superficial layers are still largely unknown.
claims.source: The mechanisms by which specific ensembles of L6 cells influence state or stimulus encoding in superficial layers are still largely unknown, and could also be mediated through a variety of intermediate cell types, layers, and brain areas that were not recorded in the present set of experiments.
claims.evidence: Acknowledgment of knowledge gap.

claims.claim: The present results directly support a specific role for L6 in the behavioral benefit of deviants.
claims.source: While the present results directly support a specific role for L6 in the behavioral benefit of deviants, and in the representation of deviation across neocortical layers, further studies are required to determine the circuit, synaptic and cellular mechanisms by which L6 affects neural encoding and behavior.
claims.evidence: Summary statement of findings.

claims.claim: The present results directly support a specific role for L6 in the representation of deviation across neocortical layers.
claims.source: While the present results directly support a specific role for L6 in the behavioral benefit of deviants, and in the representation of deviation across neocortical layers, further studies are required to determine the circuit, synaptic and cellular mechanisms by which L6 affects neural encoding and behavior.
claims.evidence: Summary statement of findings.

claims.claim: The encoding of small stimulus changes in L2/3 RS is analogous to the emergence of complex temporospatial receptive fields in upper layers of visual neocortex.
claims.source: The encoding of small stimulus changes in L2/3 RS, specifically the history dependence of these responses, is analogous to the emergence of complex temporospatial receptive fields (Martin and Whitteridge, 1984; Gilbert, 1977) and mismatch encoding (Zmarz and Keller, 2016) in upper layers of visual neocortex.
claims.evidence: Comparison to prior literature supported by citations to Martin and Whitteridge, 1984; Gilbert, 1977; Zmarz and Keller, 2016.

claims.claim: The diversity in L2/3 responses could reflect neuron types defined by biophysical characteristics or projection targets.
claims.source: The diversity in L2/3 responses, where both positive and negative change coefficients were observed, could reflect neuron types defined by biophysical characteristics (Jouhanneau et al., 2014) or projection targets, such as targeting higher somatosensory or motor cortices (Sato and Svoboda, 2010; Chen et al., 2013b), or may emerge from differential afferent connectivity.
claims.evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citations to Jouhanneau et al., 2014; Sato and Svoboda, 2010; Chen et al., 2013b.

claims.claim: The sparsity of L6 CT activity and their targeting by long-range corticocortical afferents suggests they might be gated by inputs from other higher-order neocortical areas.
claims.source: The sparsity of L6 CT activity, and their targeting by long-range corticocortical afferents (Vélez-Fort et al., 2014), suggests that they might be gated by inputs from other higher-order neocortical areas, as previously proposed (Lee et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citations to Vélez-Fort et al., 2014 and Lee et al., 2008.

claims.claim: A sparse pattern of activity in L6, comprised of both active and inactive neurons with specific connectivity, is required for deviance encoding.
claims.source: Even though weak L6 CT drive did not alter stimulus-driven firing rates, this manipulation changed the ensemble of sensory-driven neurons. This finding suggests that a sparse pattern of activity, comprised of both active and inactive neurons in L6, with specific connectivity, is required for deviance encoding.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the effects of ensemble shuffling on deviance encoding.

claims.claim: The specific population of L6 cells active during optogenetic drive was different from the one active in control conditions.
claims.source: There are two types of mechanisms by which this manipulation could lead to the observed disruption of change encoding in L2/3. The specific population of L6 cells active during optogenetic drive was different from the one active in control conditions.
claims.evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The population of L6 CT cells that is active during optogenetic drive carries less stimulus information than the population that is active in the control condition.
claims.source: Additionally, we found that the population of L6 CT cells that is active during optogenetic drive carries less stimulus information than the population that is active in the control condition (Figure 8—figure supplements 1 and 2), suggesting that any decoding of stimulus information from L6 would be impaired under the optogenetic drive condition.
claims.evidence: Supported by 2-photon imaging data in Figure 8—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claims.claim: The findings do not provide evidence for or against a specific circuit or circuits for change detection.
claims.source: Regardless of mechanism, our findings do not provide evidence for or against a specific circuit or circuits for change detection, but rather that specific activity patterns in L6 are required for the cortical architecture to perform change detection.
claims.evidence: Acknowledgment of limitations in interpretation.

claims.claim: Specific activity patterns in L6 are required for the cortical architecture to perform change detection.
claims.source: Regardless of mechanism, our findings do not provide evidence for or against a specific circuit or circuits for change detection, but rather that specific activity patterns in L6 are required for the cortical architecture to perform change detection.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the necessity of specific L6 ensembles for deviance encoding and behavior.

claims.claim: The similar findings across Gap Crossing and head-fixed paradigms suggest the mechanism could be involved in more general predictive models.
claims.source: In this study, we employed two kinds of deviants. Variations from repeating baseline stimuli applied to the vibrissae, and ethologically relevant deviations in the position of a platform in the middle of sampling by freely behaving animals. In the latter case, the stimulus statistics (mainly vibrissa identity, angles, and curvature upon touch) change continuously as the mice approach or retreat from the target platform (Voigts et al., 2008; Figure 2—figure supplement 2). In both cases, predictive models were at some level formed within the system, driving the change in response patterns and behavior. The similar findings across these paradigms suggests that the mechanism underlying the observed effects could be involved in more general predictive models.
claims.evidence: Inferred from consistency of findings across different behavioral paradigms.

claims.claim: L6 CT could be one node of the larger laminar cortical circuit for processing of higher-order stimulus features, stimulus context, or expectations reliant on top-down signaling.
claims.source: In sum, we found that stimulus encoding by specific ensembles of L6 cells is required for change encoding in L2/3 and for change-detection behavior, but not basic detection performance. These L6 CT could therefore be one node of the larger laminar cortical circuit for processing of higher-order stimulus features, stimulus context, or expectations reliant on top-down signaling, in agreement with L6 CT targeting by long-range cortico-cortical inputs (Zhang et al., 2014; Vélez-Fort et al., 2014; Vélez-Fort et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Inferred from findings and supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2014; Vélez-Fort et al., 2014; Vélez-Fort et al., 2018.

results.result: Strong optogenetic drive of L6 CT neurons (>2 mW) reduced Gap Crossing success from ~75% to ~50% and suppressed sensory gain across cortical layers, without affecting whisking patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C30, C31, C7, and C46 provide converging behavioral and electrophysiological evidence with appropriate statistical tests (p<0.01) and controls for motor confounds. The dose-dependent effect is well-characterized and consistent with prior literature (Olsen et al., 2012).

results.result: Mice detect and behaviorally respond to small platform position deviants during Gap Crossing by slowing their approach, and weak L6 drive selectively abolishes this deviant-specific behavior without affecting baseline performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35 and C38 demonstrate selective behavioral effects with appropriate sham controls and statistical significance (p<0.001 for deviant effect, p=0.9 for baseline). The dissociation between deviant and baseline performance is a key strength, though the interpretation relies on inference about the mice's perceptual state.

results.result: Direction deviants in vibrissa stimulation enhanced detection of threshold-level stimuli in head-fixed mice, and weak L6 drive eliminated this enhancement without affecting baseline detection.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 replicate the selective deviant effect in a different behavioral paradigm with controlled stimulus parameters. The convergence across two behavioral tasks strengthens the conclusion, though sample size (N=3 mice) is modest.

results.result: Weak L6 optogenetic drive (<1 mW) did not significantly alter sensory-evoked firing rates in regular-spiking neurons across cortical layers, with only modest effects on L4 fast-spiking interneurons and non-sensory L6 fast-spiking cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C53 provide detailed layer-by-layer electrophysiological analysis with appropriate statistical tests. The lack of rate changes in RS neurons (p=0.18 for L6, non-significant for other layers) is critical for interpreting subsequent ensemble effects, though the transient suppression in L2/3 (C53) warrants further investigation.

results.result: Weak optogenetic drive changed the identity of sensory-responsive L6 neurons without altering overall population firing rates, with ~25% of cells facilitated and ~24% suppressed in the laser condition.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C58 and C3 demonstrate ensemble shuffling using 2-photon imaging with statistical significance (p<0.001 for ensemble change). However, the interpretation of 'shuffling' as a mechanistic explanation requires caution—the data show correlation but not causation regarding downstream effects.

results.result: Small variations in baseline stimulus amplitude (±15%) were not encoded in mean firing rates of L4 or L2/3 regular-spiking neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61 establish that the stimulus range used does not drive amplitude encoding in baseline conditions (p=0.221 for L4, p=0.201 for L2/3). This is important for isolating deviance-specific effects, though the negative result depends on statistical power.

results.result: The stimulus design avoided pre-cortical stimulus-specific adaptation, as evidenced by the lack of overall firing rate increases for deviants when amplitude increases and decreases were grouped together.
results.evaluation: Claims C62, C63, C106, and C107 demonstrate that the experimental design successfully minimized bottom-up adaptation effects. This is a critical control for interpreting cortical contributions to deviance detection, supported by population-level data (Figure 6e).

results.result: L4 neurons consistently showed positive change coefficients, firing more for amplitude increases and less for decreases, with spike count differences larger than for baseline variations. No significant deviant encoding was observed in L5.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 and C73 characterize L4 encoding with appropriate statistics (p=0.005 for population shift, p=0.016 for comparison to baseline). The interpretation as enhanced amplitude discrimination after adaptation is reasonable, though alternative explanations are not fully excluded.

results.result: L2/3 neurons showed heterogeneous deviance encoding with both positive and negative change coefficients, representing history-dependent change signals rather than absolute amplitude tuning.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C72, C74, and C2 demonstrate L2/3 heterogeneity using multiple statistical measures (IQR p=0.006, entropy p=0.029) and a clever control for amplitude tuning (fixed deviant amplitude analysis, p=0.004). The history-dependence analysis is particularly strong.

results.result: L6 CT neurons encoded stimulus amplitude with higher calcium signals for larger stimuli, both for baseline variations and for deviants presented after adaptation, potentially serving as a baseline for change detection.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C78 establish L6 amplitude encoding using 2-photon imaging (p<0.001 for both baseline and deviant encoding). However, the slow timescale of GCaMP6s limits temporal resolution, and the interpretation of this encoding as a 'baseline for change detection' is speculative.

results.result: Weak optogenetic drive disrupted L6 CT amplitude encoding and changed the sensory-responsive ensemble despite not altering overall firing rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C79, C80, and C91 demonstrate loss of encoding with statistical significance (p<0.05) and careful controls for regression to the mean. The convergence of ensemble changes and encoding loss strengthens the conclusion, though the causal relationship between these effects remains unclear.

results.result: Weak L6 drive eliminated heterogeneous deviance encoding in L2/3, causing neurons to instead show positive change coefficients similar to L4 and reducing history-dependence.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C84, C5, and C92 demonstrate disruption of L2/3 encoding with multiple statistical measures (entropy p=0.010, IQR p=0.020, paired p=0.008). The shift toward L4-like encoding is compelling, though the mechanism linking L6 manipulation to L2/3 changes requires further investigation.

results.result: Weak L6 optogenetic drive did not significantly affect deviance encoding in VPM thalamic neurons, and layers receiving direct thalamic input showed no explicit deviance encoding beyond current amplitude, supporting a local cortical mechanism for L2/3 deviant responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C90 provide important control data ruling out thalamic contributions. The VPM recordings (N=25 responsive cells from 240 total) show no deviance encoding or modulation by L6 drive. However, the relatively small sample of responsive VPM neurons and lack of analysis of thalamic synchrony limit the strength of this negative result.

results.result: Deviant stimuli enhanced tactile detection in mice, and weak L6 optogenetic drive selectively suppressed this behavioral benefit across multiple tasks without altering baseline performance.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C4, C93, C101, and C102 synthesize behavioral findings across paradigms. The consistency of selective deviant effects is impressive, though the interpretation of 'enhancement' versus 'detection' requires careful consideration of task demands and decision criteria.

results.result: Specific ensembles of stimulus-driven L6 neurons are required for neocortical change detection and its behavioral benefit, but not for basic sensory function, indicating that specific activity patterns in L6 are necessary for cortical change detection.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C103, C111, C112, and C120 represent the manuscript's central conclusion, integrating behavioral, ensemble, and encoding data. While the convergence is compelling, the causal chain from ensemble identity to L2/3 encoding to behavior is inferred rather than directly demonstrated. The mechanism by which ensemble 'shuffling' disrupts downstream processing remains unclear, and alternative explanations (e.g., degraded information content, altered synchrony) are not fully excluded.

results.result: A sparse pattern of activity in L6, comprising both active and inactive neurons with specific connectivity, is required for deviance encoding, though the findings do not identify specific circuits for change detection.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C119 propose a mechanistic interpretation of ensemble effects. While the data support the necessity of specific L6 patterns, the interpretation of 'specific connectivity' is speculative. The acknowledgment in C119 that specific circuits are not identified is appropriate, but this limits the mechanistic insight provided.

results.result: The weak L6 manipulation isolated a network mechanism selectively involved in stimulus change processing but not in processing of repeating or predictable stimuli, contrasting with prior findings that subtle optogenetic manipulations in SI can affect baseline behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C104 and C105 highlight the specificity of the manipulation. The contrast with prior literature is well-documented, though the interpretation of 'isolation' of a specific mechanism may overstate the selectivity given the complexity of cortical circuits.

results.result: Weak L6 drive slightly increased the overall likelihood of Gap Crossing.
results.evaluation: Claim C36 reports a small increase in crossing probability with weak L6 drive. While supported by data (Figure 1d), this effect is not well-explained and could reflect non-specific arousal or attentional effects. Further investigation is needed.

results.result: Weak L6 drive disrupted encoding of deflection direction in L6 and of deviant stimuli in L2/3 in the direction-deviant paradigm.
results.evaluation: Claims C43 and C44 extend the main findings to direction deviants (Figure 3—supplement 2). The convergence across stimulus types strengthens the generality of the conclusions, though the data are presented as supplementary and less thoroughly analyzed.

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive background on neocortical evolution, predictive coding theory, deviance detection across sensory modalities, and the properties of L2/3 and L6 neurons based on prior literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C29 establish the theoretical and empirical context for the study through citations to established literature. These claims are appropriately supported by prior work and provide necessary background, though they do not constitute novel findings.

results.result: Gap Crossing is sensitive to changes in sensory function, and platform position deviants likely result from changes in multiple sensory parameters including vibrissal deflection amplitude, timing, angles, asymmetry, torque, and vibrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C37 and C39 establish the validity of the behavioral assay and characterize the complexity of the sensory deviant. The citations to prior work on vibrissal mechanics are appropriate, though the specific contributions of different parameters to deviant detection in this task are not empirically tested.

results.result: Strong L6 CT optogenetic activation recruits trans-laminar inhibition and reduces sensory gain, and optogenetic drive of L6 impacts sensory responses through an intracortical pathway rather than by modulation of thalamic relay neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C45 and C85 cite prior literature (Olsen et al., 2012; Bortone et al., 2014) to establish the known effects of strong L6 drive and the intracortical pathway. These claims provide important context for interpreting the current findings.

results.result: L4 findings can be interpreted as enhanced specificity of encoding following adaptation, consistent with enhanced discriminability of stimulus features generally observed with adaptation.
results.evaluation: Claims C67 and C68 provide an interpretation of L4 encoding patterns based on prior literature on adaptation. The interpretation is reasonable and well-supported by citations, though alternative explanations are not fully explored.

results.result: L6 CT cells may affect cortical activity via recruitment of local and trans-laminar inhibition and through corticothalamic effects, though the mechanisms by which specific L6 ensembles influence superficial layer encoding are largely unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C110 acknowledge mechanistic uncertainty while proposing potential pathways based on prior literature. The speculation is appropriately cautious, but the lack of circuit-level data limits mechanistic understanding.

results.result: The encoding of small stimulus changes in L2/3 is analogous to complex receptive fields in visual cortex, and the diversity in L2/3 responses could reflect neuron types or differential connectivity, while L6 CT sparsity suggests gating by higher-order cortical inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C115 draw analogies to visual cortex and propose speculative mechanisms for L2/3 diversity and L6 gating. These interpretations are reasonable but not directly tested, and alternative explanations are not excluded.

results.result: The similar findings across Gap Crossing and head-fixed paradigms suggest the mechanism could be involved in more general predictive models, and L6 CT could be one node of the larger laminar cortical circuit for processing higher-order stimulus features and top-down signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C121 and C122 synthesize findings across paradigms and propose a broader functional role for L6 CT. The convergence across tasks is compelling, though the generalization to 'more general predictive models' requires further testing with diverse stimulus types and behavioral contexts.

results.result: The study used NTSR1-Cre mice with viral or transgenic ChR2 expression in L6 CT neurons, with appropriate quality control to exclude aberrant expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C127 describe the experimental subjects and methods. The genetic targeting and quality control procedures are appropriate and well-documented, providing confidence in the specificity of L6 CT manipulation.
